content: Blepharitis is an inflammatory condition of the eyelids that manifests with symptoms such as itchiness, redness, flaking, and crusting. It is a common condition that affects individuals of all ages and ethnicities. While it is generally not severe, in rare cases, it can lead to permanent changes in the eyelid margin or even vision loss. This vision loss may result from complications such as superficial keratopathy (corneal abnormalities), corneal neovascularization, or corneal ulceration. Blepharitis often causes significant ocular discomfort, including a burning sensation, irritation, tearing, and redness of the eyes. It can also lead to visual disturbances such as photophobia (light sensitivity) and blurred vision. The exact cause of blepharitis is not fully understood, but it is believed to have a multifactorial origin. Potential contributing factors include chronic low-grade bacterial infections of the ocular surface, infestations with parasites like Demodex, and inflammatory skin conditions such as atopy or seborrhea. Blepharitis can be classified in several ways. One classification is based on the duration of the disease, distinguishing between acute and chronic blepharitis. Another classification is based on the anatomical location of the disease: anterior blepharitis, which affects the front of the eyelid (e.g., staphylococcal or seborrheic blepharitis), and posterior blepharitis, which involves the back of the eyelid and is often associated with meibomian gland dysfunction (MGD). This review focuses specifically on chronic blepharitis and further categorizes it into anterior and posterior types. The objective of this review was to evaluate the effectiveness of various interventions for the treatment of chronic blepharitis. To achieve this, a comprehensive search of multiple databases was conducted, including CENTRAL, MEDLINE, EMBASE, the metaRegister of Controlled Trials, ClinicalTrials.gov, and the WHO International Clinical Trials Registry Platform. The search included studies published up to February 9, 2012, and there were no restrictions on language or publication date. Reference lists of included studies were also reviewed to identify additional relevant studies. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and quasi-randomized controlled trials (CCTs) involving adults aged 16 years or older who had a clinical diagnosis of chronic blepharitis. Studies were also included if they reported separate data for participants with chronic blepharitis, even if these participants were part of a larger study population. The interventions examined in the review included medical treatments and eyelid hygiene measures. Two authors independently assessed the search results, reviewed full-text articles for eligibility, evaluated the risk of bias, and extracted data. When studies compared similar interventions and reported comparable outcomes at the same time points, the data were combined in meta-analyses. Otherwise, the results were summarized narratively. A total of 34 studies involving 2,169 participants with blepharitis were included in the review. Of these, 20 studies (14 RCTs and 6 CCTs) included 1,661 participants with anterior or mixed blepharitis, while 14 studies (12 RCTs and 2 CCTs) included 508 participants with posterior blepharitis (MGD). The studies varied widely in terms of follow-up periods, types of interventions, and participant characteristics, which limited the ability to perform meta-analyses. For anterior blepharitis, topical antibiotics were found to provide some symptomatic relief and were effective in eradicating bacteria from the eyelid margin. Lid hygiene measures, such as warm compresses and eyelid cleaning, appeared to provide symptomatic relief for both anterior and posterior blepharitis. However, the effectiveness of other treatments, such as topical steroids and oral antibiotics, was inconclusive due to insufficient evidence. Despite the inclusion of 34 trials, the review found no strong evidence to support the effectiveness of any specific treatment for curing chronic blepharitis. Many commercial products are marketed and prescribed for blepharitis without robust evidence of their efficacy. Further research is needed to evaluate the effectiveness of these treatments. Future RCTs should stratify participants by the type of blepharitis (e.g., staphylococcal blepharitis or MGD) to reduce the risk of imbalances between groups and to ensure adequate statistical power. Medical interventions and commercial products should be compared with conventional lid hygiene measures to determine their relative effectiveness. Additionally, head-to-head comparisons between treatments should be conducted. Outcomes should be patient-centered and measured using validated questionnaires or scales. Long-term follow-up, lasting at least one year, is essential to properly assess the outcomes of chronic blepharitis treatments.
